## Task 13: the generated column grows weight class B, and both spellings of the fingerprint move in one commit

Traps 2 and 3, in one migration and one commit. This is the task M6 wrote a
comment in `services/search.py` to hand over:

> **A non-empty `credits` breaks the agreement with `_FINGERPRINT_SQL`**, which
> has no credits column, and the failure is the silent one: every title with a
> credit matches the stale predicate forever. **M7 moves both sides in one commit
> or neither.** Pinned by `test_credits_are_accepted_and_are_empty_in_m6`, whose
> second assertion exists to make that visible rather than to check a string.

### There are three spellings, not two, and the third is the one that gets missed

Trap 2 names two: the Python composer and the SQL predicate. Reading the code
there is a third, and it is where an implementer who does everything the trap says
still ships the infinite backfill.

| # | Site | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `compose_document`'s assembly — `services/search.py:160-171` | the text that gets embedded, and the `md5` of it |
| 2 | `_FINGERPRINT_SQL` — `db/repositories/search.py:132-139` | the same string, spelled in SQL, over `titles`' own columns |
| 3 | **`IndexService.index`'s call site — `services/index.py:99`** | `compose_document(title)`, with `credits` left at its default `()` |

Site 3 exists because **Task 12 decided `credit_names` is not a `Title` field.**
`_to_domain` filters `DERIVED_COLUMNS` out, so the `Title` object `IndexService`
holds cannot supply the names, and `compose_document(title)` silently composes the
M6 document. Sites 1 and 2 can both move correctly and the pair still disagrees on
every credited title, forever.

**That is the cost of Task 12's decision, named rather than discovered.** The
alternative — `Title` modelling `credit_names` — makes site 3 free and buys a
domain model on which `title.evolve(credit_names=…)` spells an array that
disagrees with the `credits` table. The trade is one indexed single-row read per
index job, on a path that then runs a 65 MB ONNX model at ~83 texts/s, against a
domain type that can express a lie. Take the read.

So the port grows a batch accessor, and it is on `TitleRepository` because
`credit_names` is a column of `titles`:

```python
@abstractmethod
async def credit_names_for(
    self, title_ids: Sequence[uuid.UUID]
) -> dict[uuid.UUID, tuple[str, ...]]:
    """Weight class B's input for a page of titles.

    **Not a field on `Title`, and this method is the consequence.**
    `credit_names` is in `DERIVED_COLUMNS` -- it is `credits` projected to
    names and truncated to a ranking constant, so a domain model carrying it
    would be a cast list that is not the cast, on the object
    `GET /titles/{id}` hydrates from. The composer needs it anyway, because
    the fingerprint it computes has to reproduce `_FINGERPRINT_SQL` byte for
    byte and that predicate reads the column.

    Batch, so the backfill pays one read per page rather than one per title.
    A title with no credits is present in the answer with an empty tuple, not
    absent: the assembly is **positional** and an absent key would be spelled
    as a missing segment, which is precisely failure mode (a) in
    `services/search.py`'s module docstring.
    """
```

### The `if credits:` in `compose_document` is already the forbidden shape

Read the shipped composer's last two lines before changing anything:

```python
    if credits:
        text = text + _SECTION + _ITEM.join(credits)
```

That is **conditional appending**, and `services/search.py`'s own module docstring
lists it first among *"three shapes of the obvious Python composer [that] are
unreproducible in SQL and all three are refused here"*:

> 1. *Appending a section only when the field is populated.* `_FINGERPRINT_SQL`
>    is `coalesce(..., '')` on every nullable column with no conditionals, so it
>    emits six segments for every title. The assembly below is positional for that
>    reason: **a missing overview is an empty line, never an absent one.**

The M6 shim is in violation of the rule its own module states — harmlessly, because
`credits` was always `()` so the branch never taken. **Task 13 must not carry it
forward.** The seventh segment is unconditional, and it moves from the end of the
assembly to position three, matching the generated column's concatenation order so
that all three spellings read in the same sequence:

```python
    text = _SECTION.join(
        (
            title.name,
            title.original_name or "",
            _ITEM.join(credits),
            title.overview or "",
            title.tagline or "",
            _ITEM.join(title.genres),
            _ITEM.join(title.keywords),
        )
    )
```

and, matching it exactly:

```python
_FINGERPRINT_SQL = """md5(
    coalesce(t.name, '')             || CHR(10) ||
    coalesce(t.original_name, '')    || CHR(10) ||
    usher_array_text(t.credit_names) || CHR(10) ||
    coalesce(t.overview, '')         || CHR(10) ||
    coalesce(t.tagline, '')          || CHR(10) ||
    usher_array_text(t.genres)       || CHR(10) ||
    usher_array_text(t.keywords)
)"""
```

`usher_array_text` on both sides, never a hand-rolled join: the module docstring's
failure mode (2) says this schema has *"one definition of 'an array as text' …
rather than two"*, and `_ITEM` is already declared to be that wrapper's separator.
Verified on pg17.10 that the empty case agrees: `usher_array_text(ARRAY[]::text[])`
returns `''` and `md5(usher_array_text(ARRAY[]::text[])) = md5('')` is true, so a
title with no credits produces the identical empty segment on both sides.

### The test that catches moving one alone, and why the existing cross-check is not enough

The existing cross-check is
`tests/integration/test_search_repository.py::test_the_composer_and_the_sql_fingerprint_agree`,
and its body is:

```python
    assert compose_document(title).fingerprint == await _sql_fingerprint(session, title.id)
```

**It calls `compose_document` with the default `credits=()` and seeds a title with
no credits, so it is green under every wrong implementation this task can
produce.** Move only the SQL: the seeded title's `credit_names` is `{}`, both
sides emit an empty segment, the strings match. Move only the Python: the same,
because the composer is called without credits. Move both and forget site 3: it
still calls the composer directly, so site 3 is not in the picture at all. The
case is correct and load-bearing for what it was written for, and it cannot see
any of this.

Two new cases. The first extends the cross-check to the population that can
disagree:

**`test_the_composer_and_the_sql_fingerprint_agree_for_a_title_with_credits`** —
seed a title with a populated `credit_names`, call
`compose_document(title, credits=<those names>)`, compare against
`_sql_fingerprint`. Kills sites 1 and 2 moving apart, in either direction.

The second is the one that actually names the failure, and it asserts the
**closure property** rather than an equality of two strings:

**`test_an_indexed_title_with_credits_stops_matching_the_stale_predicate`** —
seed a title with credits, run `IndexService.index` over it, then assert
`count_stale(model) == 0`. Trap 2's failure spelled out:

> Move only the Python side and every credited title matches the stale predicate
> **forever**: the backfill re-embeds it, writes a fingerprint the SQL cannot
> reproduce, and re-claims it on the next pass. **An infinite backfill that never
> errors.**

That is a loop, not an exception. Nothing raises, `usher index` reports a
plausible stale count that never reaches zero, the worker is busy, and
`usher.embedding.duration` looks healthy because the embeds are real. **The only
observable is the one this case asserts**: after indexing, the title stops
matching. It is also the only case that catches site 3, and it is worth writing
the site-3 bug deliberately and watching it fail before fixing it — the count
comes back `1`, twice in a row, from a handler that returned successfully.

`test_credits_are_accepted_and_are_empty_in_m6` is deleted in this commit. Its
docstring says it exists *"to make that visible rather than to check a string"*,
and the thing it was making visible has now happened. Deleting it is the correct
ending; leaving it asserting `credits == ()` would pin the milestone shut.

### The migration: the forced rewrite, quoted from the migration that carries it

`fa2b6c1e9d30`'s docstring, verbatim, under the heading **CHANGING THE WRAPPER'S
BODY REQUIRES A FORCED REWRITE IN THE SAME MIGRATION**:

> `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` does not recompute stored generated values —
> verified directly: a row stored as `'alpha':1 'beta':2` did not move when the
> body changed, while a fresh evaluation returned something else, and a subsequent
> `UPDATE` of that row *did* recompute it. So a replaced body produces a table
> where some rows were computed by the old definition and some by the new, with
> nothing to tell them apart and the split decided by which rows happened to be
> touched since. The recipe, in this order, in one migration:
>
> ```
> op.drop_index("ix_titles_search_document", table_name="titles")
> op.execute("ALTER TABLE titles DROP COLUMN search_document")
> op.execute("CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION usher_array_text ...")
> op.execute("ALTER TABLE titles ADD COLUMN search_document ... STORED")
> op.create_index("ix_titles_search_document", ...)
> ```
>
> Drop-and-re-add rather than `UPDATE titles SET id = id`: both force a full
> rewrite, but the update also leaves 1.27M dead tuples and their WAL behind for
> autovacuum. Either way it is a table rewrite on the whole catalog, so it is a
> maintenance window and not a hot deploy.
> `tests/integration/test_search_document.py::test_the_stored_document_equals_a_freshly_computed_one`
> is what catches a migration that forgets.

**M7 uses four of those five steps.** The wrapper's body does not change — the
expression does — so `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION usher_array_text` is omitted and
its omission is stated in the docstring, because a reader who has been told the
recipe is five steps and finds four will otherwise assume a mistake.

**One measured alternative, recorded so it is not rediscovered as a fix.**
PostgreSQL 17 has `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … SET EXPRESSION AS (…)`, and
measured on pg17.10 it does everything this needs in one statement: it rewrote the
table, recomputed every row under the new expression, **preserved the GIN index
including its `WITH (fastupdate=off)` reloption**, kept the index usable
(`Bitmap Index Scan on ix_t5_doc` after the change), and left
`count(*) WHERE doc IS DISTINCT FROM (<fresh expression>)` at zero. PRD 01 pins
the stack at *"PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector ≥ 0.8.5"*, so it is available.

**Declined, for one reason.** The drop-and-re-add recipe is already written down,
already reversible in `fa2b6c1e9d30`'s `downgrade()`, and works for the *other*
change this schema will eventually make — a wrapper body change, which
`SET EXPRESSION` does not help with because the function must be replaced first
and every row recomputed after. Two recipes for one hazard is how the wrong one
gets used on the case it does not cover. Recorded as measured-and-declined rather
than unconsidered, with the numbers, so a later milestone can reverse it on
evidence.

### The intended consequence: the whole enriched tier re-embeds, at once

This is trap 2's second half and it is not a bug:

> And note the *intended* consequence of moving both: every fingerprint in the
> enriched tier changes at once, so the whole tier re-embeds — which is ADR-0020's
> scheme working, not a bug, and is 25 s to 2 min at the measured throughput.

**Every fingerprint, including titles with no credits**, and the reason is the
positional assembly: an uncredited title gains a seventh empty segment, which is
one more `\n` in the hashed string. There is no subset of the catalog that keeps
its old fingerprint. `services/search.py` already priced this:

> **Changing the assembly invalidates every stored vector, on purpose.** Add a
> field, change a separator, reorder a section — every fingerprint moves, every
> row matches the stale predicate, and the backfill re-embeds the enriched tier in
> the 25 s to 2 min it costs (~8,000-10,700 tokens/s on CPU, ~100-130 tokens a
> document). **That is the scheme working, not a migration to write.**

The operator sequence after this lands is therefore `alembic upgrade head` →
`usher derive --backfill` → `usher index --backfill` → `usher work`, **in that
order**, and the order matters: indexing before deriving embeds every title with
an empty class B and then re-claims all of them once `credit_names` is populated,
which is the wasted pass twice over. Task 38's live run follows this order and
records the actual wall time against the 25 s–2 min estimate.

Note also the **document is now longer**, so the token estimate `usher index`
prints is low by the length of the credit list. Ten names at ~2 tokens is ~20
tokens on a ~115-token document, so the printed range is ~17% optimistic. Either
update the constant in `cli.py:_index` or record the discrepancy; do not leave a
number that was measured for a different document shape presented as if it were
still measured.

### The weights, and what the new class does to the ranking cases

The expression's classes after this task: **A** = `name`, `original_name`;
**B** = `credit_names`; **C** = `overview`, `tagline`; **D** = `genres`,
`keywords`. B slots between A and C, which is where `fa2b6c1e9d30` reserved it —
*"Weight B is reserved for cast and crew and is deliberately absent rather than
filled with something else"*.

**`test_a_name_match_outranks_an_overview_match` stays green and is not enough.**
It compares A against C, and B sits between them without touching either. A
milestone that filled B with the wrong weight — `'A'`, say, or `'D'` — passes it.

**A new contract case is needed, and it was measured before being written.** On
pg17.10, three rows carrying the term `Marlow Vance` in three different classes,
scored with `ts_rank(search_document, websearch_to_tsquery('english','marlow
vance'))`:

| Where the term is | Class | `ts_rank` |
|---|---|---|
| the title's `name` | A | **0.9910322** |
| the title's `credit_names` | B | **0.39641288** |
| the title's `overview` | C | **0.19820644** |

A is 2.5× B and B is 2× C, with no ties and no tuning — those are the default
`ts_rank` weights `{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}` doing exactly what the class assignment
says. So:

**`test_a_cast_match_ranks_below_a_name_match_and_above_an_overview_match`**,
in `tests/contract/search_index_contract.py` beside the existing case, so it runs
against `FakeSearchIndex` **and** `PostgresSearchIndex`. It asserts on *position*,
seeding all three rows in one index — the front matter's rule 1, and here it is
what distinguishes "B is between A and C" from "B exists". Two wrong
implementations it kills: class B filled at `'A'` (the cast match ties the name
match, and the assertion is an ordering not a membership), and class B filled at
`'D'` (it falls below the overview match).

**The fake has to learn about it.** `tests/fakes/search_index.py`'s docstring
already names `test_a_name_match_outranks_an_overview_match`, so it carries a
weight model rather than a substring check, and a class it does not model makes
the new case fail against the fake while passing against Postgres — which is a
green integration run and a red unit run, and is the correct order to fix them in.
**Check `ports/search.py`'s `SearchDocument` before writing the case**: if its
weight classes are named fields rather than a mapping, it needs a `credits` field
and that is part of this commit, not a follow-up.

## Task 14: `list_in_progress`, `list_recent`, and the recency key `ix_watch_states_user_played` does not have

Continue Watching is *"in progress for user X, most recent first"*, and the layer
answers neither half. There is no in-progress statement at all, and
`ix_watch_states_user_played` is `(user_id, played)` — an equality pair with **no
recency column**, so `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC` over a household's states is a
full sort of the per-user set on every home screen, every 60 seconds, forever.

**And the index is very likely read by nothing today, which changes what this task
does to it.** Every statement in `db/repositories/watch_state.py` was read for this
plan: `_NEEDING_HISTORY` is `WHERE played AND play_count = 0 ORDER BY updated_at,
id` — it leads with `played` and leaves `user_id` unconstrained, so a
`(user_id, played)` btree cannot serve it. `_get` is `WHERE user_id = :user_id AND
{target} = :target_id`, served by `uq_watch_states_user_title` /
`uq_watch_states_user_episode`. `_update` and `_insert` drive off those same two
unique constraints. That leaves nothing. If it holds, `ix_watch_states_user_played`
is `ix_titles_popularity` again — an index M1 declared for a query that was never
written — and the right move is not to add a recency index *beside* it but to
**replace it**, since `(user_id, played, last_played_at)` is a strict prefix
superset of `(user_id, played)` and serves everything the narrow one could.
**Step 1 proves that claim with `EXPLAIN` before Task 17 acts on it**; a plan that
drops an index on the strength of a grep is how a nightly job loses its plan.

### `NULLS`, and why this is the trap rather than the sort

`last_played_at` is nullable and ADR-0014 is why: a walk's *listing* frequently
cannot determine it, so a walk-sourced state carries `NULL` and a push-sourced one
carries a real instant. Two facts then compose into a silent wrong answer:

1. **Postgres orders `DESC` as `NULLS FIRST` by default.** So the obvious
   `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC` puts **every walk-sourced state above every
   push-sourced one** — Continue Watching leads with precisely the rows the system
   knows least about, and the row is populated, plausible and wrong. This is the
   front matter's whole thesis arriving on line one of the first statement.
2. **`NULLS LAST` in the query and `DESC` in the index do not match.** A btree
   declared `(user_id, played, last_played_at DESC)` is `NULLS FIRST` and cannot
   supply `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST` as an ordered scan — Postgres
   silently adds a `Sort` node and the index buys the scan bound and nothing else.
   The index must be declared **`last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST`**, spelled out, or
   the recency half of this task is decorative.

So the settled ordering is `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC`, and
the index Task 17 creates is `(user_id, played, last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST)`.

**`updated_at` is deliberately not in that ORDER BY, and its absence is a decision.**
`trg_watch_states_set_updated_at` is a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger assigning `now()`
unconditionally, so `updated_at` is *the write instant*, not the watch instant.
Under a nightly walk `now()` is frozen per transaction, so a million merged rows
share one `updated_at` and it is a no-op tiebreak; under a push it is approximately
the request instant, which is a fact about Usher rather than about the household.
`id DESC` (UUIDv7, so creation order) at least means "the most recently created
state", which is a fact about the household. `updated_at` as the *primary* key
would be worse still, and the repository module already records that this column is
the trigger's, not the statement's.

### What "in progress" means, settled

There is no `in_progress` column. `NOT played AND position_seconds > 0` is the
obvious definition and it is the one this port takes, with its known cost stated
rather than papered over: **a title opened and abandoned at 3 seconds is in
progress forever.** There is no dismissal affordance anywhere in PRD 06 or PRD 07,
so nothing ever clears it.

**The floor belongs in the provider, not in the predicate**, for three reasons that
compound:

- A floor is a product tunable (`position_seconds > 60`? `> 2% of runtime`?), and a
  tunable inside a **partial index predicate** makes every change to it a migration
  plus an index rebuild.
- The percentage spelling needs `runtime_seconds`, which is **nullable** — so
  `position_seconds::float / runtime_seconds > 0.02` is `NULL` (and therefore
  false) for every state whose runtime the source did not report, silently
  emptying Continue Watching on a source that reports no runtimes.
- Postgres can use a partial index when the query's predicate **implies** the
  index's. A loose index predicate (`NOT played AND position_seconds > 0`) with a
  tighter provider predicate (`AND position_seconds > 60`) still uses the index; the
  reverse does not. So putting the floor in the provider costs nothing and putting
  it in the index costs a migration per adjustment.

The port's docstring says "in progress" means the durable fact and the provider
owns the floor, so Task 24 has no design left to make.

### One method or two — two, and a third in Task 16

`list_in_progress` and `list_recent` are **two methods**, and the reason is not
symmetry:

| | `list_in_progress` | `list_recent` |
|---|---|---|
| predicate | `NOT played AND position_seconds > 0` | `played` |
| target | titles **and** episodes | rolled up to titles only |
| return | `WatchState` (the resume target's own identity) | `RecentWatch` (a rolled-up title) |
| consumer | `ContinueWatchingProvider` | `BecauseYouWatchedProvider` seeds, `TasteService` |

One method with `played: bool` and four optional filters is a query builder wearing
a port method's name. Task 16 adds a **third**, `list_rediscoverable`, for the same
reason.

**`list_recent` serves both its consumers with one method and different limits.**
`TasteService` wants ~50 recent watches to average; `BecauseYouWatchedProvider`
wants ~3 seeds. Same predicate, same ordering, same dedup — only `limit` differs, so
splitting them would be two spellings of one statement, which is trap 2's shape one
subsystem over.

### `list_recent` rolls episodes up to their series; `list_in_progress` does not

This asymmetry is the part that reads as an oversight if it is not written down.

**`list_recent` must roll up.** 999,827 of the one measured source's 1,126,674
items are episodes, so on a TV-heavy household nearly every `played` state is keyed
on `episode_id`. `title_embeddings` and `title_neighbors` are both keyed on
`titles.id`; an episode has neither. A title-only `list_recent` therefore returns an
empty list for exactly the household PRD 06's taste model is meant to describe, and
`TasteService` computes a centroid over nothing — which composes into a home screen
that is populated, plausible and personalised to no one. So the statement is
`LEFT JOIN episodes e ON e.id = ws.episode_id` and the key is
`COALESCE(ws.title_id, e.title_id)`.

**And the rolled-up value cannot be a `WatchState`.** `WatchState`'s model
validator requires exactly one of `title_id`/`episode_id`, and the CHECK
`num_nonnulls(title_id, episode_id) = 1` says the same thing in the database. A row
carrying the *series'* `title_id` and the *episode's* `episode_id` is unconstructible,
and one carrying the series' `title_id` alone is a lie about which row was read. So
`list_recent` returns a new `RecentWatch` value object in `ports/repository.py`,
beside `BulkWriteResult` and `SweepResult`, which is where this project already puts
a port's own result shape.

**The dedup is mandatory, not defensive.** Ten watched episodes of one series roll
up to ten rows with one `title_id`. Without `DISTINCT ON` the three
`BecauseYouWatched` seeds are three copies of one show, and the taste centroid is
the mean of one series counted ten times. Same argument `_EXTERNAL_IDS_FOR_TITLES`
and `media_item.py`'s `DISTINCT ON` comments already make.

**`list_in_progress` must *not* roll up**, because the resume target is the episode
itself. Collapsing an in-progress episode to its series card loses the identity the
client needs to resume, and `ContinueWatchingProvider` (Task 24) is where one card
per series is decided — stated on the port so it is not decided twice.

# tests/contract/watch_state_repository_contract.py  (append)


async def _seed_progress(
    repository: WatchStateRepository,
    user_id: uuid.UUID,
    title_id: uuid.UUID,
    *,
    last_played_at: datetime | None,
    position_seconds: int = 90,
    played: bool = False,
) -> None:
    await repository.merge_from_source(
        [
            merge(
                user_id,
                title_id,
                position_seconds=position_seconds,
                played=played,
                last_played_at=last_played_at,
            )
        ]
    )


class WatchStateRepositoryInProgressContract:
    """`list_in_progress` and `list_recent`, the two reads Continue Watching
    and the taste centroid are built on.

    Kept as a separate mixin from `WatchStateRepositoryContract` only so the
    two integration subclasses can seed the extra titles these need without
    every merge case paying for them.
    """

    async def test_in_progress_excludes_a_title_that_was_finished(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """The distractor the front matter names for ContinueWatching: a title
        finished last night, which carries `played = true` and
        `position_seconds = 0` and is the single most recent thing the
        household did.

        The wrong implementation this kills: `WHERE user_id = :u` with no
        `played` predicate at all, which is what an implementation written
        against the *index* (`user_id, played`) rather than against the
        *question* produces -- it has the column available and never filters
        on it.
        """
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, title_id, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED)
        await _seed_progress(
            repository,
            user_id,
            other_title_id,
            last_played_at=LATER,
            position_seconds=0,
            played=True,
        )

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [title_id]

    async def test_in_progress_excludes_a_title_at_position_zero(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """`NOT played AND position_seconds > 0`, both halves.

        A state at `position_seconds = 0` and `played = false` is a title the
        source knows about and nobody has started -- which on a full walk is
        most of the library. The wrong implementation this kills is
        `WHERE NOT played` alone, which returns the household's entire
        unwatched catalog in physical order and satisfies every
        `len(rows) > 0` assertion anyone will ever write about it.
        """
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, title_id, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED)
        await _seed_progress(
            repository, user_id, other_title_id, last_played_at=None, position_seconds=0
        )

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [title_id]

    async def test_in_progress_is_ordered_by_recency_and_not_by_insertion_order(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
        third_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """Three rows, inserted A B C, watched B A C.

        `watch_states.id` is a UUIDv7, so insertion order *is* id order, and
        the point of the permutation is that neither direction of an id sort
        produces the expected answer: `ORDER BY id` gives A B C and
        `ORDER BY id DESC` gives C B A, and the correct answer is B A C. A
        fixture seeded in watch order would be satisfied by both an id sort
        and a recency sort, which is the failure the contract table names --
        "ordered by `id` ... is *satisfied by a seeded fixture inserted in the
        right order*".

        The wrong implementations this kills: `ORDER BY id DESC`,
        `ORDER BY id`, and no ORDER BY at all (physical order, which on a
        fresh table is insertion order and therefore also A B C).
        """
        oldest = LAST_PLAYED
        middle = LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(days=2)
        newest = LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(days=5)

        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, title_id, last_played_at=middle)  # A
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, other_title_id, last_played_at=newest)  # B
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, third_title_id, last_played_at=oldest)  # C

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [other_title_id, title_id, third_title_id]

    async def test_a_state_with_no_last_played_at_does_not_outrank_one_that_has_one(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """The trap of this task, pinned.

        `last_played_at` is nullable because ADR-0014 says a walk's listing
        frequently cannot determine it -- so on a walk-sourced library it is
        `NULL` on nearly every row, and on a push-sourced one it is a real
        instant. Postgres's default for a `DESC` sort is **NULLS FIRST**, so
        the obvious `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC` hoists every state the
        system knows *least* about to the top of Continue Watching, forever,
        on a row that is populated and plausible and indistinguishable from
        working.

        `NULLS LAST` is therefore not tidiness. The wrong implementation this
        kills is exactly one missing word, and there is no other assertion in
        this suite that can see it.

        It also fixes the *other* direction as a decision: a state that cannot
        be dated sorts last rather than being dropped, because dropping it
        would empty Continue Watching entirely on a walk-only deployment.
        """
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, title_id, last_played_at=None)
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, other_title_id, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED)

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [other_title_id, title_id]

    async def test_in_progress_is_scoped_to_one_user(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """A household is per-person (PRD 02's `User` docstring), and the
        wrong implementation is a `WHERE` clause that lost its first
        predicate -- which on a single-user deployment, i.e. every
        deployment during development, is undetectable."""
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, title_id, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED)
        await _seed_progress(repository, other_user_id, other_title_id, last_played_at=LATER)

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [title_id]

    async def test_in_progress_returns_an_episode_state_without_rolling_it_up(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        episode_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """The asymmetry with `list_recent`, asserted rather than commented.

        Continue Watching's card resumes a *file*; an episode state collapsed
        to its series' `title_id` has lost the only identity a client can
        resume from. `list_recent` rolls up and this does not, and a reader
        who finds one of the two and infers the other is wrong either way.
        """
        await repository.merge_from_source(
            [merge(user_id, None, episode_id=episode_id, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED)]
        )

        rows = await repository.list_in_progress(user_id)

        assert [row.episode_id for row in rows] == [episode_id]
        assert rows[0].title_id is None

    async def test_recent_rolls_an_episode_up_to_its_series(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        episode_id: uuid.UUID,
        episode_series_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """999,827 of the one measured source's 1,126,674 items are episodes,
        so a title-only `list_recent` returns an empty list for a TV-heavy
        household -- and `TasteService` then averages nothing and
        `BecauseYouWatchedProvider` seeds from nothing, which composes into a
        home screen that is populated, plausible, and personalised to no one.

        `title_embeddings` and `title_neighbors` are both keyed on
        `titles.id`; an episode has neither, which is why the rollup is here
        rather than in the two services.

        The wrong implementation this kills: `WHERE title_id IS NOT NULL`,
        which is the natural spelling and is green on every movie fixture.
        """
        await repository.merge_from_source(
            [
                merge(
                    user_id,
                    None,
                    episode_id=episode_id,
                    played=True,
                    last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED,
                )
            ]
        )

        rows = await repository.list_recent(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [episode_series_id]

    async def test_recent_returns_one_row_per_series_however_many_episodes_were_watched(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        episode_ids: list[uuid.UUID],
        episode_series_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """`BecauseYouWatchedProvider` emits one row *per seed*. Without the
        dedup, a household that watched ten episodes of one show gets ten
        identical "Because you watched" rows, and the taste centroid is the
        mean of one series counted ten times -- a centroid that is
        confidently wrong rather than empty, which is worse.

        The wrong implementation this kills: the rollup without the
        `DISTINCT ON`.
        """
        for index, episode in enumerate(episode_ids):
            await repository.merge_from_source(
                [
                    merge(
                        user_id,
                        None,
                        episode_id=episode,
                        played=True,
                        last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(hours=index),
                    )
                ]
            )

        rows = await repository.list_recent(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [episode_series_id]
        assert rows[0].last_played_at == LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(hours=len(episode_ids) - 1)

    async def test_recent_excludes_something_still_in_progress(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """`played`, not "has a `last_played_at`". A seed for "because you
        watched" that names a film the household abandoned twenty minutes in
        is a recommendation built on a rejection.

        The wrong implementation this kills: reusing `list_in_progress`'
        predicate with a different ORDER BY, which is what "one method with a
        flag" degenerates into.
        """
        await _seed_progress(
            repository, user_id, title_id, played=True, last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED
        )
        await _seed_progress(repository, user_id, other_title_id, last_played_at=LATER)

        rows = await repository.list_recent(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [title_id]

    async def test_recent_is_ordered_by_recency_and_not_by_insertion_order(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
        third_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """The same A-B-C / B-A-C permutation as the in-progress case, for the
        same reason and against a different statement.

        The front matter's own example of a silent wrong answer is
        "`BecauseYouWatchedProvider` seeded from the *oldest* watch state
        rather than the most recent returns a beautifully constructed row
        about a film watched in 2019". `ORDER BY last_played_at` without
        `DESC` is that bug, one word long, and only an ordering assertion on a
        deliberately-permuted fixture can see it.
        """
        oldest = LAST_PLAYED
        middle = LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(days=2)
        newest = LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(days=5)

        await _seed_progress(
            repository, user_id, title_id, played=True, last_played_at=middle
        )
        await _seed_progress(
            repository, user_id, other_title_id, played=True, last_played_at=newest
        )
        await _seed_progress(
            repository, user_id, third_title_id, played=True, last_played_at=oldest
        )

        rows = await repository.list_recent(user_id)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [other_title_id, title_id, third_title_id]

    async def test_recent_respects_its_limit(
        self,
        repository: WatchStateRepository,
        user_id: uuid.UUID,
        title_id: uuid.UUID,
        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,
        third_title_id: uuid.UUID,
    ) -> None:
        """One method, two consumers, different limits: `TasteService` wants
        ~50 to average, `BecauseYouWatchedProvider` wants ~3 seeds. If the
        limit were not honoured they would be two methods, and this is the
        case that says so.

        Note the limit is applied *after* the dedup: a limit pushed inside the
        `DISTINCT ON` returns fewer than `limit` distinct titles whenever a
        series is involved, which on a TV household is always.
        """
        for index, identifier in enumerate((title_id, other_title_id, third_title_id)):
            await _seed_progress(
                repository,
                user_id,
                identifier,
                played=True,
                last_played_at=LAST_PLAYED + timedelta(days=index),
            )

        rows = await repository.list_recent(user_id, limit=2)

        assert [row.title_id for row in rows] == [third_title_id, other_title_id]

# tests/integration/test_watch_state_repository.py  (append)


async def test_the_in_progress_statement_has_no_sort_node_once_the_index_exists(
    session: AsyncSession, repository: PostgresWatchStateRepository, user_id: uuid.UUID
) -> None:
    """Scoped to the stage that has an ordering to serve, per the standing
    rule: this asserts the absence of a `Sort` **above the index scan on
    `watch_states`**, not the absence of a `Seq Scan` anywhere in the plan. An
    unscoped "no Seq Scan" assertion fails on a three-row fixture for a plan
    that is correct at a hundred thousand rows, and a suite that has to
    disable that assertion has learned nothing.

    `SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off` is what makes the claim observable at
    all on a near-empty table -- the same technique
    `test_a_fuzzy_lookup_uses_the_trigram_index` uses one file over.

    The wrong implementation this kills is the one this task exists to
    prevent: an index declared `(user_id, played, last_played_at DESC)`
    without `NULLS LAST`. That index serves the *filter* and cannot supply
    the *order*, so Postgres inserts a `Sort` -- which is invisible in every
    behavioural case in this file, because the answer is correct either way.
    """
    await session.execute(text("SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off"))
    result = await session.execute(
        text(
            "EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM watch_states "
            "WHERE user_id = CAST(:user_id AS uuid) AND NOT played AND position_seconds > 0 "
            "ORDER BY last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC LIMIT 20"
        ),
        {"user_id": user_id},
    )
    plan = "\n".join(row[0] for row in result)
    assert "ix_watch_states_user_recent" in plan, plan
    assert "Sort" not in plan, plan

class RecentWatch(NamedTuple):

    schema actually has.

    Not a `WatchState`, and that is structural rather than stylistic: a
    watched *episode* is rolled up to its series here, and a `WatchState`
    carrying a series' `title_id` alongside an episode's `episode_id` is

    `play_count` is here rather than being left for a second call because it
    is the only engagement signal `watch_states` carries -- there is no
    rating column (M7 front matter) -- and every consumer of this method
    wants to weight by it.

    last_played_at: datetime | None

    @abstractmethod
    async def list_in_progress(
        self, user_id: uuid.UUID, *, limit: int = 20
    ) -> list[WatchState]:
        """One user's in-progress states, most recently played first.

        **"In progress" is `NOT played AND position_seconds > 0`**, and both
        halves are load-bearing. Without `NOT played`, a title finished last
        night is the single most recent thing the household did and heads the
        row. Without `position_seconds > 0`, the answer is the entire
        unwatched library in physical order -- which is a populated, plausible
        row that satisfies every `len(cards) > 0` assertion ever written
        about it.

        **A minimum position is deliberately *not* here.** A title abandoned
        at three seconds is in progress by this definition and stays there
        forever, because nothing in PRD 06 or PRD 07 can dismiss a card. The
        floor belongs to `ContinueWatchingProvider`: it is a product tunable,
        the percentage spelling needs the nullable `runtime_seconds` (and so
        evaluates to false for every state whose runtime a source did not
        report), and Postgres uses a partial index whenever the query's
        predicate implies the index's -- so a tighter provider predicate over
        this looser one costs nothing, while a floor baked into the index
        predicate makes every adjustment a migration.

        **Ordered `last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC`.** `NULLS LAST` is
        the whole correctness content of that clause: `last_played_at` is
        nullable because a walk's listing frequently cannot determine it
        (ADR-0014), Postgres's default for `DESC` is NULLS FIRST, and the
        obvious spelling therefore ranks every state the system knows least
        about above every state it knows most about. `updated_at` is not a
        tiebreak here: it is trigger-owned and is the *write* instant, which a
        nightly walk makes identical across a million rows because `now()` is
        frozen per transaction.

        **Episode states are returned as themselves, not rolled up to their
        series.** The card resumes a file. Collapsing to one card per series
        is the provider's, and is decided once, there.
        """

    @abstractmethod
    async def list_recent(
        self, user_id: uuid.UUID, *, limit: int = 20
    ) -> list[RecentWatch]:
        """One user's most recently *finished* titles, one row per title.

        Feeds `BecauseYouWatchedProvider`'s seeds and `TasteService`'s
        centroid. One method rather than two: same predicate, same ordering,
        same dedup, and only `limit` differs (~3 seeds against ~50 to
        average).

        **`played`, not "has a `last_played_at`".** A seed naming a film the
        household abandoned twenty minutes in is a recommendation built on a
        rejection.

        **Watched episodes are rolled up to their series' `title_id`, and this
        is not a convenience.** `title_embeddings` and `title_neighbors` are
        keyed on `titles.id` and an episode has neither, while 999,827 of the
        one measured source's 1,126,674 items are episodes -- so a title-only
        implementation returns an empty list for exactly the household PRD
        06's taste model describes, and both consumers then produce confident
        output from no input.

        **One row per title.** Ten watched episodes of one series are one
        seed, or `BecauseYouWatchedProvider` emits ten identical rows and the
        centroid is one series counted ten times. `last_played_at` and
        `play_count` come from the most recent contributing state.

        Ordered `last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST`, with the same `NULLS`
        argument as `list_in_progress`. `limit` is applied after the dedup: a
        limit pushed inside it returns fewer than `limit` distinct titles
        whenever a series is involved.

```python
# src/usher/db/repositories/watch_state.py  (modify -- module level)

# Continue Watching. `NOT played AND position_seconds > 0` is the port's
# definition of "in progress"; the *floor* (a minimum position, or a
# percentage of runtime) is deliberately the provider's, because Postgres can
# use a partial index whenever the query predicate implies the index
# predicate, so a tighter caller costs nothing and a tighter index costs a
# migration per adjustment.
#
# ORDER BY: `NULLS LAST` is the correctness content, not the formatting.
# `last_played_at` is nullable (ADR-0014 -- a walk's listing cannot determine
# it), Postgres defaults a DESC sort to NULLS FIRST, and the natural spelling
# therefore puts every walk-sourced state above every push-sourced one. The
# index this reads, `ix_watch_states_user_recent`, is declared
# `last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST` for the same reason: a DESC-NULLS-FIRST
# btree serves the filter and cannot supply this order, so the planner adds a
# Sort and the recency key buys nothing.
#
# No `updated_at` tiebreak: it is owned by trg_watch_states_set_updated_at
# and is the write instant, which a full walk makes identical across a
# million rows because `now()` is frozen per transaction.
#
# `CAST(:user_id AS uuid)`, never `:user_id::uuid` -- SQLAlchemy's `text()`
# bind regex skips a name followed by `::` and the literal reaches asyncpg.
# And no `:word` anywhere in these comments: the same regex scans comment
# lines, so a colon-name in a `--` comment declares a real bind parameter the
# caller must then supply.
_IN_PROGRESS = """
SELECT * FROM watch_states
WHERE user_id = CAST(:user_id AS uuid)
  AND NOT played
  AND position_seconds > 0
ORDER BY last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC
LIMIT :limit
"""

# `BecauseYouWatched` seeds and the taste centroid.
#
# The LEFT JOIN is what makes this work on a real library: 999,827 of the one
# measured source's 1,126,674 items are episodes, `title_embeddings` and
# `title_neighbors` are keyed on titles.id, and an episode has neither -- so
# without the rollup this returns nothing for a TV household and both
# consumers compute confidently from an empty set.
#
# The inner DISTINCT ON is mandatory rather than defensive, exactly as it is
# in media_item.py: ten watched episodes of one series are one seed. The
# outer level re-sorts because DISTINCT ON forces its own ORDER BY to lead
# with the distinct key, so the recency order has to be applied again above
# it -- which also means this statement's ordering is a Sort node by
# construction and the index bounds the *scan*, not the sort. That is bounded
# by the household's watch history, not by the catalog.
#
# `WHERE title_id IS NOT NULL` on the outer level, not the inner: an episode
# whose series row was deleted rolls up to NULL, and filtering it inside the
# DISTINCT ON would let a *second* state for the same series win the slot.
_RECENT = """
SELECT title_id, last_played_at, play_count FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (COALESCE(ws.title_id, e.title_id))
           COALESCE(ws.title_id, e.title_id) AS title_id,
           ws.last_played_at AS last_played_at,
           ws.play_count AS play_count
    FROM watch_states ws
    LEFT JOIN episodes e ON e.id = ws.episode_id
    WHERE ws.user_id = CAST(:user_id AS uuid) AND ws.played
    ORDER BY COALESCE(ws.title_id, e.title_id),
             ws.last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, ws.id DESC
) newest
WHERE title_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY last_played_at DESC NULLS LAST, title_id DESC
LIMIT :limit
"""
```

```python
# src/usher/db/repositories/watch_state.py  (modify -- PostgresWatchStateRepository, append)

    async def list_in_progress(
        self, user_id: uuid.UUID, *, limit: int = 20
    ) -> list[WatchState]:
        with self._session.no_autoflush:
            rows = (
                (
                    await self._session.execute(
                        text(_IN_PROGRESS), {"user_id": user_id, "limit": limit}
                    )
                )
                .mappings()
                .all()
            )
        return [WatchState.model_validate(dict(row)) for row in rows]

    async def list_recent(self, user_id: uuid.UUID, *, limit: int = 20) -> list[RecentWatch]:
        with self._session.no_autoflush:
            rows = (
                await self._session.execute(text(_RECENT), {"user_id": user_id, "limit": limit})
            ).all()
        return [RecentWatch(row.title_id, row.last_played_at, row.play_count) for row in rows]
```

## Task 15: `EpisodeRepository.next_up` — the join that exists nowhere in `src/`

**There is no join from `watch_states` to `episodes` anywhere in the repository
today.** Not one. `watch_state.py` never mentions `episodes`; `episode.py` never
mentions `watch_states`. There is no batch `get_for_episodes`, and
`list_for_title` returns the entire tree — 20,000 rows for the one measured
pathological series. So this is a **new statement**, not a new caller of an old
one, and `NextUpProvider` must never reach for `list_for_title`: a provider asking
about two hundred started series through it reads four million rows to produce two
hundred cards.

### "Next up" settled: a high-water mark, not a gap

Two semantics are defensible and they diverge on a case every household hits.

- **First gap.** Return the earliest unplayed episode that follows the earliest
  played one. A user who skipped S02E05 — a clip show, a crossover, an episode
  that would not play — is told to watch S02E05 tonight, and tomorrow, and every
  night after, because there is no dismissal affordance anywhere in PRD 06 or
  PRD 07. The row is populated, correct-looking, and permanently stuck.
- **High-water mark.** Take the greatest `(season_number, episode_number)` among
  played episodes and return the one immediately after it. A skipped episode is
  skipped; the household moves on.

**High-water wins**, and the loser is recorded because a reader who assumes "next"
means "first gap" will read the statement as a bug. The cost of high-water is
stated too: an episode watched out of order *ahead* of the household's position —
a finale spoiled, a pilot rewatched — moves the mark forward and silently skips
everything between. That is recoverable by watching the skipped episodes (which
does not move the mark backward, but also does not need to); the gap semantic's
failure is not recoverable at all.

**"Last played" is a position in the series, not the most recent instant.** The
mark is `max(season_number, episode_number)` over played episodes, never
`ORDER BY last_played_at DESC LIMIT 1`. A household that finishes S03 and then
rewatches the pilot is not asking to be told to watch S01E02, and `last_played_at`
is nullable besides — on a walk-sourced library it is `NULL` on nearly every row,
so a recency-keyed implementation returns nothing at all for most series, which
reads as "everything is finished".

### The three edge cases, each settled and each with a case

**The finale — return nothing, never wrap.** When no episode has a
`(season_number, episode_number)` greater than the mark, the series is finished and
the provider has nothing to say. Wrapping to S01E01 produces the front matter's
named silent failure verbatim: *"a `NextUpProvider` that returns a series' first
episode instead of its next one returns a valid, populated, correctly-shaped row —
forever, silently, for every series in the library."* The strict `>` row comparison
is what makes "nothing after the mark" and "nothing at all" the same answer, which
is why the statement uses one rather than hand-expanding it.

**Nothing played — return nothing, not S01E01.** PRD 06 fires this provider on
*"Series with an unwatched next episode"*. A series never started has no *next*
episode; it has a *first* one, which is a different claim. And the arithmetic
decides it independently: at 32,409 series, "S01E01 of everything unstarted" is a
Next Up row containing the household's entire unwatched television library in
whatever order the planner produced it — the generic-row failure the front matter's
rule 2 names, wearing a personalised row's title. Never-started series are
`RecentlyAdded`'s and M9's `/browse`'s. **Recorded in PRD 06 in the same commit**,
because the table's "Fires when" column currently reads as though it might mean
either.

**Specials are season 0, and they are excluded from both sides.** The CHECK is
`season_number >= 0`, so season 0 is legal and TMDb uses it for specials. Left in:
a household that watched one Christmas special has a mark of `(0, 1)`, so Next Up
offers S01E01 and presents "start this show" as "continue it"; and a special could
itself be returned as the next episode, which is an out-of-band bonus presented as
the next chapter. The lexicographic ordering `(0, n) < (1, 1)` is an artefact of
how the numbering is spelled, not a claim about viewing order — a special has no
defined position in the narrative sequence, which is what season 0 *means*.
So `season_number > 0` appears on both the mark side and the candidate side.
**Named because its absence is otherwise indistinguishable from having forgotten
it**, which is this schema's own idiom for a deliberate exclusion. PRD 06 says
nothing about specials today; the decision goes there.

### Which side of the watch-state key

Watch state on an episode is keyed on **`episode_id`**; a series' own state is keyed
on **`title_id`**. This statement needs the `episode_id` side and must not read the
other, and the repository already records the shape of the mistake: `media_item.py`
notes that `title_id` alone answers *the whole show* and that `AND episode_id IS
NULL` is the bound, because an episode's row carries its series' `title_id` too.

Here the hazard runs the other way and is worse. A source can set a series-level
`played = true` (Emby will, when a user marks a show watched). An implementation
that reads `watch_states` by `title_id` sees one played row and concludes the series
is finished — so `NextUpProvider` goes silent for that show forever, which is an
*absent* row rather than a wrong one and therefore leaves nothing at all to notice.
The join is `ws.episode_id = e.id`, which excludes title-keyed rows structurally
rather than by predicate, since `uq_watch_states_user_episode` treats NULLs as
distinct and an equality join never matches one.

### Many series in one statement

`NextUpProvider` asks about every series the household has started. A per-series
loop is the N+1 this task exists to prevent, and it is the same defect
`resolve_seasons`' docstring already argues against ("a per-title signature is one
round trip per series in the batch, which at 999,827 episodes is the same design
defect batching exists to avoid"). So the signature takes a list of series and
returns a mapping:

```
next_up(user_id, title_ids: Sequence[UUID]) -> dict[UUID, Episode]
```

Two `DISTINCT ON`s, one statement:

```sql
WITH mark AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (e.title_id)
           e.title_id AS title_id, e.season_number AS season_number,
           e.episode_number AS episode_number
    FROM watch_states ws
    JOIN episodes e ON e.id = ws.episode_id
    WHERE ws.user_id = CAST(:user_id AS uuid)
      AND ws.played
      AND e.title_id = ANY(CAST(:title_ids AS uuid[]))
      AND e.season_number > 0
    ORDER BY e.title_id, e.season_number DESC, e.episode_number DESC
)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (e.title_id) e.*
FROM mark m
JOIN episodes e
  ON e.title_id = m.title_id
 AND (e.season_number, e.episode_number) > (m.season_number, m.episode_number)
WHERE e.season_number > 0
ORDER BY e.title_id, e.season_number, e.episode_number
```

`max()` over a composite is not available in Postgres, which is why the mark is a
`DISTINCT ON` rather than a `GROUP BY`. The **row comparison** `(a, b) > (c, d)` is
the load-bearing spelling: it is lexicographic by definition, and the hand-expanded
`e.season_number > m.season_number OR (e.season_number = m.season_number AND
e.episode_number > m.episode_number)` is the same thing written three ways to get
wrong. It is also what keeps the statement indexable — a btree row comparison
against `(title_id, season_number, episode_number)` is pushed down as an index
condition, and that index already exists as `uq_episodes_title_season_episode`.

### `EXPLAIN`, and the finding that this statement needs no new index

`uq_episodes_title_season_episode` is `(title_id, season_number, episode_number)`
and serves both halves: the mark side seeks on `title_id = ANY(...)`, the candidate
side takes the row comparison as an index condition under the nested loop.
`uq_watch_states_user_episode` is `(user_id, episode_id)` — `user_id` is a single
value and `episode_id` is the join key, so the probe is an index lookup with both
columns bound. **Nothing here wants an index that does not already exist**, and that
is a result rather than an omission: Task 17's whole discipline is that an index
nothing reads is `ix_titles_popularity` again, and the way to avoid adding one here
is to `EXPLAIN` first and record the plan.

`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` this statement at scale in `scripts/measure_rows.py`
(Task 17 owns the script) and paste the plan into the migration's docstring under
the heading **"indexes this migration deliberately does not add"**. The expected
shape at a household scale — 32,409 series, 999,827 episodes, ~50,000 played states,
200 probed series — is two index scans and a nested loop, with no seq scan of
`episodes`. If it is not, the finding belongs to *this* task, before Task 17 is
tempted to index around it.

**The plan assertion in the suite is scoped**, per the standing rule: it asserts
`uq_episodes_title_season_episode` appears and that no `Seq Scan on episodes`
appears, under `SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off`, and it says nothing about the rest
of the plan — an unscoped "no Seq Scan anywhere" fails on a fixture of six episodes
for a statement that is correct at a million.

# tests/integration/test_episode_repository.py  (append)


async def test_next_up_reads_the_episode_key_index_and_does_not_scan_episodes(
    session: AsyncSession, user_id: uuid.UUID, series_id: uuid.UUID
) -> None:
    """Scoped to the stage with an ordering to serve, per the standing rule:
    `uq_episodes_title_season_episode` must appear and `Seq Scan on episodes`
    must not. Nothing is asserted about the rest of the plan, because a
    six-episode fixture seq-scans whatever it is given and an unscoped
    assertion would be a claim about the fixture.

    This is also the case that justifies **not** adding an index in Task 17.
    The row comparison `(season_number, episode_number) > (...)` is pushed
    down as an index condition against the existing unique constraint; the
    hand-expanded `OR` form is not, and would make this a filter over the
    whole series. Both spellings return identical rows, so nothing else can
    tell them apart.
    """
    await session.execute(text("SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off"))
    result = await session.execute(text(f"EXPLAIN {_NEXT_UP}"), {...})
    plan = "\n".join(row[0] for row in result)
    assert "uq_episodes_title_season_episode" in plan, plan
    assert "Seq Scan on episodes" not in plan, plan
```

# src/usher/ports/repository.py  (modify -- EpisodeRepository, after list_for_title)

    @abstractmethod
    async def next_up(
        self, user_id: uuid.UUID, title_ids: Sequence[uuid.UUID]
    ) -> dict[uuid.UUID, Episode]:
        """The next episode to watch for each of many series, in one round
        trip.

        **"Next" is the episode immediately after the household's high-water
        mark** -- the greatest `(season_number, episode_number)` among played
        episodes of that series -- not the first gap. A skipped episode stays
        skipped: nothing in PRD 06 or PRD 07 can dismiss a card, so a
        gap-seeking implementation makes one skipped episode this household's
        Next Up tonight and every night after.

        **The mark is a position, not an instant.** Never
        `ORDER BY last_played_at DESC LIMIT 1`: a household that finishes
        season three and rewatches the pilot is not asking for S01E02, and
        `last_played_at` is nullable on nearly every walk-sourced row
        (ADR-0014), which makes a recency-keyed mark arbitrary rather than
        merely wrong.

        **Absent, not null, in three cases**: nothing played (a series never
        started has a *first* episode, not a next one -- and "S01E01 of
        everything unstarted" is the whole unwatched library wearing a
        personalised row's title); the mark is the finale (the series is
        finished; **never wrap to S01E01**); and no episodes at all. A key
        missing from the mapping means "nothing to say", which is the answer
        PRD 06 asks a provider to give.

        **Season 0 is excluded on both sides.** Specials are out-of-band by
        construction, and `(0, n) < (1, 1)` is an artefact of the numbering
        rather than a claim about viewing order -- so one watched special
        must not make this say "continue" about a show nobody has started,
        and a special must never be offered as the next chapter.

        **Reads watch state keyed on `episode_id` only.** A series' own
        `title_id`-keyed row is the whole show, and a source can set it
        (Emby's "mark series watched"); an implementation that reads it
        concludes the series is finished and goes silent for that show
        forever.

        **One statement for every series asked about.** A per-series loop
        returns the identical mapping and is the N+1 this method exists to
        prevent -- the same argument `resolve_episodes` makes, and the reason
        `NextUpProvider` must never reach for `list_for_title`, which returns
        the whole tree (20,000 rows for the measured pathological series).
        """
```

Add `_NEXT_UP` to `db/repositories/episode.py` exactly as given in the section
above, with the reasoning carried in a module comment (high-water not gap; row
comparison not hand-expanded `OR`, and that this is what keeps
`uq_episodes_title_season_episode` usable as an index condition; `season_number > 0`
on both sides; `DISTINCT ON` because `max()` over a composite does not exist;
`ws.episode_id = e.id` and never `title_id`). **No `:name` token inside any `--`
comment in that module** — SQLAlchemy's bind regex scans comment lines, so a
colon-name there declares a bind parameter the caller must supply, and the failure
is a `StatementError` about a missing parameter that names a column.

```python
# src/usher/db/repositories/episode.py  (modify -- PostgresEpisodeRepository, append)

    async def next_up(
        self, user_id: uuid.UUID, title_ids: Sequence[uuid.UUID]
    ) -> dict[uuid.UUID, Episode]:
        if not title_ids:
            return {}
        with self._session.no_autoflush:
            rows = (
                (
                    await self._session.execute(
                        text(_NEXT_UP),
                        {"user_id": user_id, "title_ids": list(dict.fromkeys(title_ids))},
                    )
                )
                .mappings()
                .all()
            )
        return {row["title_id"]: Episode.model_validate(dict(row)) for row in rows}
```

## Task 16: recently-added and rediscover, and the rating column that does not exist

Two reads, one on each of the two tables Group E touches, and they fail in opposite
directions: `list_recently_added` has a column and no index and no bound, and
`list_rediscoverable` has an index it can borrow and **no column at all** for half
of what PRD 06 asks it to express.

### `list_recently_added`

`media_items.added_at` exists, is nullable, and is **unindexed** — `source.py`'s own
comment says so and defers it ("no index on added_at/last_seen_at/available …
revisit for M9"). The only statement reading it today is `list_unmatched`, hard
filtered to `title_id IS NULL`: the review queue, which is the complement of what
this provider wants.

**The bound is a time window, not a row count, and PRD 06 already says so** —
`RecentlyAddedProvider` fires on *"New items in the window"*. That choice is what
makes the dedup affordable, so it has to be settled before the statement is written.

**Deduplicated to one row per title, and `episode_id IS NULL` is deliberately *not*
how it is done here.** An episode's `MediaItem` carries its series' `title_id`
(`media_item.py` records this three times), so a series that just landed produces
one row per episode file — 20,000 rows for the measured pathological series, one
card. Three shipped statements bound that with `episode_id IS NULL`, and
`_OWNED_TITLE_IDS`' comment measures the alternative at 20,001 rows read to answer
one boolean. **Here the same bound is the wrong one**, and its cost is named on the
port already: *"a library that reported episodes but never their series row reads as
not-owned for that series."* Recently Added is precisely the surface where a newly
added series must appear, and a household whose source reports episode files and no
series-level row would never see one. So this statement takes `DISTINCT ON
(title_id)` over *all* matched rows, and takes the window as the bound instead:

```sql
SELECT title_id, added_at FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (title_id) title_id, added_at
    FROM media_items
    WHERE available
      AND title_id IS NOT NULL
      AND added_at >= CAST(:since AS timestamptz)
    ORDER BY title_id, added_at DESC
) newest
ORDER BY added_at DESC, title_id DESC
LIMIT :limit
```

The pathological series still contributes 20,000 rows to the scan and 1 to the
result — **that is the same 20,001-vs-1 measurement, paid inside a window instead of
across the table**, and it is the right place to pay it: 20,000 episode files that
landed last night *are* one card, and collapsing them is the work, not the waste.
Measured in Step 6 with and without the window so both numbers exist.

**`:since` is the caller's, not the statement's, and the frozen clock is why.**
`now()` is frozen per transaction and the integration fixture is one transaction, so
a statement spelling its own `now() - interval '30 days'` cannot be tested at its
boundary — every row the case inserts shares the transaction's instant, and "added
inside the window" and "added at the window's edge" become the same fact.
`clock_timestamp()` would be the statement instant and would make the test
nondeterministic instead. Passing the cutoff in removes the clock from the statement
entirely, which is also what lets `RecentlyAddedProvider` own the window as a
tunable rather than a migration.

**No `user_id`.** Availability is household-wide, so this is the one provider whose
output is identical for every member of the household. Correct, and worth stating on
the port so nobody adds a user parameter that filters nothing.

### `added_at` is not "never overwritten", and the brief's phrasing is the safe reading of a less safe statement

The shipped upsert is `added_at = COALESCE(excluded.added_at, media_items.added_at)`
(`media_item.py`, the `DO UPDATE SET` clause). That refuses to overwrite **with
NULL** — a delta payload that omits the field cannot erase it, which is the reason
the module's docstring gives. It does **not** refuse to overwrite with a *value*: if
a source reports a different `added_at`, the new one wins, every walk.

So the two consequences are opposite and both belong on the port:

- **A library re-imported into the same source keeps its dates**, as long as the
  source keeps reporting the same ones. Recently Added does not flood. This is the
  behaviour the COALESCE is usually credited with.
- **A library re-imported such that the source reports *fresh* dates** — files
  genuinely re-copied, so their creation time is new; or a source migration that
  re-derives `DateCreated` from the import — **reprograms every row's `added_at` to
  the import instant, and Recently Added becomes the entire library.** The window
  and the `LIMIT` cap how bad it looks; nothing prevents it.

**M7 does not change the COALESCE**, and the reason is that the same clause is what
lets a source that initially could not report `added_at` fill it in on a later walk.
Making the column insert-only would fix the flood and make that permanently
unfixable, which is the worse trade against a nullable column on a review-queue
table. The behaviour is recorded on the port and in PRD 02 in this commit, so the
next person to read "COALESCEd forward" does not read it as "immutable".

### Rediscover, and the substitution

PRD 06 fires `RediscoverProvider` on *"Watched > 2 years ago, **rated highly**"*.
**There is no rating column on `watch_states`, no `favorite`, and `SourceWatchState`
carries neither** — the front matter settles that M7 does not invent one. So this
task ships a **substitution**, and says so in PRD 06 in the same commit rather than
shipping a row that quietly means something else.

The available signals are `played`, `play_count`, `position_seconds`,
`runtime_seconds`, `last_played_at`. The substitution splits them:

- **The filter is `played AND last_played_at < :before`.** Reliable, and both halves
  are needed: `played` excludes something abandoned (an abandonment is a rejection,
  not a fondness), and the cutoff is the whole "> 2 years ago".
- **The engagement proxy is the *ordering*, not the filter**:
  `ORDER BY play_count DESC, last_played_at DESC`. A rewatch is a revealed
  preference and it is the only thing in this table a household writes more than
  once — which is the entire content of "rated highly" that this schema can express.

**Putting `play_count >= 2` in the filter is the tempting version and it is wrong**,
because `play_count` is not trustworthy until the history backfill has drained.
`list_needing_history`'s own docstring says `played AND play_count = 0` is how
"history unknown" is spelled, and the port records that Emby's listing reports
`PlayCount: 0` for an item played twice. So a `play_count >= 2` filter returns
**nothing** on a freshly-walked deployment — an empty row, which is at least honest,
right up until the backfill half-drains and the row starts appearing for an
arbitrary subset. As an *ordering* the same unreliable column degrades gracefully:
an un-backfilled household gets a correct set ordered by recency-within-the-old-set,
a backfilled one gets rewatches first, and neither is empty for a reason nobody can
see.

**`last_played_at` being nullable does the right thing here for free, which is the
exact mirror of Task 14.** `last_played_at < :before` is `NULL` — and therefore not
true — for every state that cannot be dated, so an undatable state is excluded from
Rediscover automatically. In Task 14's `ORDER BY` the same nullability did the
*wrong* thing for free (NULLS FIRST hoists them to the top). Same column, same
three-valued logic, opposite outcomes, and both are worth a sentence because a
reader who internalises one will get the other backwards.

**Title-keyed only, and this is not the same call Task 14 refused.** `list_recent`
had to roll episodes up because a title-only implementation returns an **empty** set
for a TV household and the taste centroid is then computed from nothing — a
correctness failure that produces confident output. `list_rediscoverable` filtered
to `title_id IS NOT NULL` produces a **correct but film-only** row: everything in it
is genuinely a thing the household watched long ago. That is a scope decision, not a
defect, and it is the right one — a "rediscover" card for a series is an invitation
to re-watch sixty hours, and PRD 06's own example is film-shaped. Recorded in PRD 06
so the absence of television from that row is a decision on the page.

### The indexes: one new, and one borrowed

**`ix_media_items_recently_added`** on `(added_at DESC NULLS LAST)`, partial
`WHERE available AND title_id IS NOT NULL`. Both halves of the predicate are in
every call, and the partial form matters at 1,126,674 rows where the unmatched
review queue and the retracted items are dead weight for this query.

**And it has an unflattering number that must be measured, not guessed.** The
predicate includes `available`, which the nightly sweep writes:
`UPDATE media_items SET available = false WHERE source_id = … AND available AND
last_seen_at < …`. Every row that sweep retracts is a row **removed from this
partial index**, so the sweep gets slower. `f1a7d3c9e824` measured that statement at
173 ms without its own index and 102 ms with it, at 1,126,674 rows with 200 stale.
**Re-measure it with this index present.** If the 102 ms moves materially, the
non-partial `(added_at DESC NULLS LAST)` — bigger, but untouched by the sweep — is
the alternative, and the choice is then a number rather than a preference.

**Rediscover gets no index of its own.** Its predicate is `user_id = :u AND played
AND last_played_at < :before`, which is an equality pair plus a range on the third
column of Task 14's `ix_watch_states_user_recent` — and a btree is bidirectional, so
a `DESC NULLS LAST` index serves a `<` range perfectly well. The `ORDER BY
play_count DESC` cannot be served and becomes a `Sort` node; that sort is over
*titles this household watched more than two years ago*, which is bounded by the
household's history and not by the catalog. **`EXPLAIN` it and record the plan**, so
"the index it borrows is enough" is an observation rather than an assumption. This
is the second of Task 17's two "deliberately not added" findings.

        )

        self,

        other_title_id: uuid.UUID,

        asserted as an *ordering*.

        predicate: `list_needing_history` records that `played AND play_count
        = 0` is how "history unknown" is spelled, and Emby's listing reports
        `PlayCount: 0` for an item played twice -- so `play_count >= 2` as a
        filter returns nothing on a freshly-walked deployment and an
        arbitrary subset on a half-backfilled one. As an ordering the same
        column degrades gracefully.

        the case above and empties this one.
